reply.title: Why does a sigmoid squash any number into 0 to 1?
reply.story:
When modeling probabilities or neural networks, we often need to take any real number—ranging from negative infinity to positive infinity—and map it smoothly into a restricted range between zero and one. Early statisticians and biometricians faced this exact problem when studying population growth, where growth starts slow, accelerates, and eventually plateaus due to carrying capacity. 

To capture this bounded behavior, they turned to the logistic function, a classic sigmoid curve. The magic of the sigmoid lies in its exponential structure. As the input grows larger and larger positively, the denominator grows exponentially faster than the numerator, pushing the output closer and closer to one. Conversely, as the input drops deeply into negative numbers, the exponential term vanishes, leaving the fraction to approach zero. 

At the exact midpoint, the output hits one half, serving as the central pivot of the S-shaped transition. By adjusting the steepness parameter, we can make this transition happen over a razor-thin window or stretch it out into a gentle slope. This makes the sigmoid an essential tool for turning raw continuous scores into clean, interpretable probabilities.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how the logistic sigmoid function squashes any input $x$ into an output between zero and one. Adjust the steepness $k$, midpoint $x_0$, and marker position to inspect the curve and its slope.
